title: Time in contact with reality
opening: An inquiry can spend more time preparing or waiting between useful contacts than the contact itself takes. Shortening one interval may fit more attempts before time or resources run out, but a relevant answer still has to change what you do next.

labels.comparison: Compare the time between useful contacts
labels.comparisonIntro: This illustration holds preparation and contact time steady across ten attempts. Change only the waiting interval and see how many contact windows fit before the same resource limit.
labels.waitQuestion: Waiting interval before the next contact

labels.interpretTitle: A shorter interval is not the whole result
labels.interpretText: A person or condition has to be able to answer the question you are asking. After contact, interpret the response and carry the useful part into the next attempt. A longer, relevant observation can teach more than several quick contacts that do not address the question.
labels.practiceIntro: Choose one question from work you are doing or considering. Mark the preparation, contact and waiting that stand between you and an answer. Keep required preparation and time-sensitive work; change only what the evidence supports.

labels.sourceQuote: Draw two timelines for the same ten attempts to test an idea. On each, mark the time when a person or real condition can respond to what you made, then mark the preparation and waiting before the next contact. Draw a line where your available time or resources run out. Hold contact duration equal in this illustration so you can see what changing the intervals does; actual tests may take different amounts of time. Which route lets you resolve more attempts before that limit?
labels.sampleLoaded: Example loaded. Replace it with your own observations when useful.

fields.label: The question and the person or condition that could answer it
What must be prepared, what happens at contact and what waits afterward
The time or resources available, and where they end
What waiting could be reduced without rushing necessary preparation or contact
How you will interpret the response and use it in the next attempt

example.question: Suppose I need to learn whether people looking for a quiet study space can find one nearby. A short conversation with someone who is looking answers a different question than showing the idea to friends.
example.route: I need to decide what to ask and where to find a relevant person. The contact itself may take longer than the conversation; I should include that time instead of assuming every test has the same duration.
example.boundary: Suppose I have one afternoon and enough time for two conversations. This is a planning example, not a measured result.
example.next: I could prepare one clear question once and reduce the delay between conversations. I would not skip the time needed to find people who can answer it.
example.reuse: After each conversation, I will separate what the person said from what I inferred and revise the next question if it did not address the uncertainty.
